 Demand for a more than double monthly minimum wage
High prices…Wages freeze for 3rd year
 Police hardline response to violent protests
 Clothing plants disrupted operations 사진 확대 In Dhaka, Bangladesh's capital, police are arresting a garment worker who participated in a demonstration to raise the minimum wage. [AFP Yonhap News] Large-scale protests have continued for a fourth day, sparked by demands by Bangladeshi clothing workers to more than double their minimum wage. Local authorities have also taken a hard-line response to a series of protesters occupying roads and setting fire to vehicles.
 According to AFP on the 2nd (local time), thousands of Bangladeshi clothing workers have been protesting for four days since the 30th of last month. They are demanding that the monthly minimum wage be raised from the current 12,500 takas (about $100) to 30,000 takas (about $241). This is 140% higher than the current minimum wage.
 They complain that it is difficult to make a living with current wages as living costs such as food, cooking gas, and electricity bills rise. In fact, according to the Bangladesh National Statistical Office, the average annual inflation rate reached 8.8% last year, followed by an 8.34% year-on-year increase in September this year. On the other hand, the legal minimum wage for garment workers has remained the same for about three years since it was raised from 8,000 to 12,500 a month in December 2023.
 사진 확대 Protests against Bangladeshi clothing workers' minimum wage increase sparked on the 30th of last month (local time) spread to major clothing production bases, including the capital, Dhaka, and northern Ghazipur and Ashlia. [AFP Yonhap News] Protests spread to major clothing production bases, including the capital Dhaka, as well as northern Ghazipur and Ashlia. In Ghazipur, hundreds of workers occupied highways and damaged vehicles. Some protesters set fire to police vehicles.
 The Bangladesh government initially sought to resolve the situation through dialogue and system improvement. On the 1st, it announced the establishment of a wage committee to review the minimum wage, and Prime Minister Tariq Rahman also held an emergency ministerial meeting to order workers to guarantee their rights and improve their living standards.
 Despite the government's conciliatory measures, however, the protests hardly subsided. In the wake of violent actions by protesters, Interior Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that he would strongly respond to illegal activities under the guise of the labor movement. Eventually, the police mobilized tear gas and flash bombs to disperse protesters, and in the process, residents reportedly suffered damage, including the spread of tear gas to nearby residential areas.
 As protests gradually spread across the country, Bangladesh's economy was also on alert. According to the industry, operations were disrupted at 679 out of 2,134 clothing factories nationwide on the 1st, or about 30%. There are concerns that the protests could also affect clothing exports.
 Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of clothing after China. As clothing exports account for more than 80% of total exports, prolonged protests are also expected to put pressure on the implementation of contracts with overseas clothing companies.
